newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil could handle $15 bln trade gap - Cenbank.
newsitem.headline: Brazil could handle $15 bln trade gap - Cenbank.

text.p: Brazil's trade deficit in 1997 is likely to be about $10 billion but could go as high as $15 billion without posing a threat to economic stability, a Central Bank director said.

"I think this year's (trade deficit) will be beneath $10 billion but, if it reaches $15 billion, there's no cause for concern," the Central Bank's monetary policy director Francisco Lopes told newspaper O Estado de Sao Paulo.
In an interview published Sunday, Lopes said Brazil's foreign currency reserves, currently around $60 billion, were more important than the trade deficit, which was being financed.
"From the Central Bank's point of view, the key variable...is the position of our foreign currency reserves and the balance of payments situation as a whole," Lopes told Estado.
"To say that there is an imbalance, that it's getting worse and we're going to explode soon if there's no drastic correction, is clearly an exaggeration," he said.

Some analysts have expressed concern that Brazil's burgeoning trade deficit, which in 1996 reached $5.54 billion, will force the government to either brake economic growth or devalue the country's Real currency.

Lopes said Brazil's trade gap was in fact a sign that industry was investing to become more competitive, and added that the upcoming privatization of the telecommunication sector would add signficantly to imports.

"Is that a worry? The answer is no because the widening (of the trade gap) will have been financed by direct investment. What I want to emphasize is that worries about the trade gap have to be put into context," he said.
"Of course, in the long term, the country cannot go on getting further into debt. But in the long term, lots of things can happen," Lopes said.
The Central Bank director recognized that Brazil's dependence on foreign capital to plug its current account deficit left it vulnerable.

"If there were a serious foreign (confidence) crisis, like in 1982, and we were suddenly cut off from international capital markets, then things would get complicated," he said. "We know we're running a risk, but it's a calculated risk."

On the fiscal front, Lopes conceded Brazil had made less progress than expected in 1996 with the nominal public sector deficit falling to six percent of GDP from seven percent in 1995. Another one percent drop in 1997 would be "a victory" and a three percent deficit was only feasible in 1999.
"Fiscal improvement is going to be gradual in Brazil. We can't expect miracles," he said, citing a freeze on public sector pay in 1996 as a tough but important measure.

The government would only consider a 1997 increase once it had seen the impact of a recent supreme court ruling that gave 11 civil servants a 28.9 percent pay rise and opened the possibility of similar, sector-wide increases, Lopes said.
